narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Modern line dance emerged in the 20th century, drawing on 19th-century European folk traditions and American physical education curricula.
Key developments include the 1957 'Madison', the 1970s disco-era 'Electric Slide', and the 1990s country-western boom sparked by 'Achy Breaky Heart'.
on_screen: Map: United States · Global
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Line dance serves as a social activity and a recreational sport.
It is used for community building in social clubs and as a structured exercise format in sports associations.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage: Line-Dance Videos (https://archive.org/details/Line-danceVideos)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers stand in parallel lines, repeating a fixed sequence of steps.
Movements are performed individually without physical contact.
Dancers rotate to face different 'walls' (front, back, sides) based on the specific choreography.
Watch for Electric Slide.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (9BhPdnxD6Xk)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Parallel lines; dancers move in unison.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Historically tied to country-western music, the genre now encompasses pop, disco, Latin, rock, and techno.
Music is typically chosen for its steady, repetitive beat that aligns with the 32, 48, or 64-step sequences.
Listen for the Country instrumentation, Synthesizers, Percussion.
The pulse is 4/4 (common) or 3/4 (waltz).
Recognizable by a consistent, driving beat that supports repetitive step patterns, often featuring a blend of acoustic country elements or electronic pop production.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Ric Silver (choreographer of the Electric Slide), Max Perry, Jo Thompson Szymanski, and Scott Blevins.
Variations include contra-style (lines facing each other) and diverse regional adaptations of country-western, such as the 'Western Swing' and 'Honky Tonk' styles.
Derived from European folk dances and 20th-century American show dance; influenced by ballroom, disco, and global pop music.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Line dance is variant of Contra dance: Contra dance involves lines facing each other, whereas standard line dance usually involves lines facing the same direction.
